claim: Genetic factors account for the majority of the variance of human bone mass.
source: Genetic factors account for the majority of the variance of human bone mass, but the contribution of non-genetic factors remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about bone mass variance.

claim: The gut microbiome is a communicable regulator of bone structure and turnover in mice.
source: We show that the gut microbiome is a communicable regulator of bone structure and turnover in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB) negatively impact skeletal maturation.
source: In addition, we found that the acquisition of a specific bacterial strain, segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB), a gut microbe that induces intestinal Th17 cell expansion, was sufficient to negatively impact skeletal maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Transfer of SFB-like microbes during therapeutic FMT procedures could lead to significant bone loss in fecal material recipients.
source: Moreover, the transfer of SFB-like microbes capable of triggering the expansion of human Th17 cells during therapeutic FMT procedures could lead to significant bone loss in fecal material recipients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: Low bone mineral density (BMD) results from suboptimal skeletal maturation culminating in low peak bone density by 30 years of age, and/or by accelerated bone loss thereafter.
source: Low bone mineral density (BMD), a key feature of osteoporosis, results from suboptimal skeletal maturation culminating in low peak bone density by 30 years of age, and/or by accelerated bone loss thereafter.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about bone mineral density and osteoporosis.

claim: Most of the variation in peak BMD is attributed to genetic heterogeneity.
source: Interestingly, there is considerable natural variation in peak BMD within populations, with most of the variation being attributed to genetic heterogeneity (Boudin et al., 2016; Peacock et al., 2002; Estrada et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The composition and community structure of the gut microbiome is a well-recognized determinant of phenotypic variability within populations.
source: A well-recognized determinant of phenotypic variability within populations is the composition and community structure of the gut microbiome (Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013; Tremaroli and Bäckhed, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mice raised in germ-free (GF) conditions have altered BMD, bone volume and bone structure compared to conventionally raised (Conv.R) mice.
source: Among them are the reports that mice raised in germ-free (GF) conditions have altered BMD, bone volume and bone structure compared to conventionally raised (Conv.R) mice (Sjögren et al., 2012; Novince et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The gut microbiome affects the bone waste induced by estrogen deficiency.
source: Additional evidence showing that the microbiome is a significant regulatory factor for skeletal health include reports that the gut microbiome affects the bone waste induced by estrogen deficiency (Li et al., 2016), glucocorticoids (Schepper et al., 2020) and by diabetes (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presence of the gut microbiota is required for parathyroid hormone (PTH) to stimulate both bone formation and bone resorption.
source: Furthermore, we showed that the presence of the gut microbiota is required for parathyroid hormone (PTH) to stimulate both bone formation and bone resorption (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Antibiotic treatment which depletes the gut microbiome increases bone density in mice.
source: It is also known that antibiotic treatment which depletes the gut microbiome increases bone density in mice (Yan et al., 2016), while bacterial recolonization post-antibiotic treatment results in bone loss (Schepper et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bacterial recolonization post-antibiotic treatment results in bone loss.
source: It is also known that antibiotic treatment which depletes the gut microbiome increases bone density in mice (Yan et al., 2016), while bacterial recolonization post-antibiotic treatment results in bone loss (Schepper et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Variations in the composition of the microbiome affect not only BMD, but also bone strength by its actions on bone material properties.
source: Moreover, variations in the composition of the microbiome affect not only BMD, but also bone strength by its actions on bone material properties (Guss et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Humans are initially colonized by microbes at birth, with the microbiota eventually reaching maturity at about 3 years of age.
source: Humans are initially colonized by microbes at birth, with the microbiota eventually reaching maturity at about 3 years of age (Yatsunenko et al., 2012; Rodríguez et al., 2015; Kashtanova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gut bacterial species adapt within individual microbiomes enabling their long-term colonization into adulthood.
source: Thereafter, gut bacterial species are thought to adapt within individual microbiomes enabling their long-term colonization into adulthood (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Early microbial colonization and microbiota succession is influenced by the maternal microbiota.
source: Early microbial colonization and microbiota succession is influenced by the maternal microbiota, although a precise measure of the extent to which a mother microbiome is acquired by the offspring has been challenging to ascertain (Benson et al., 2010; McKnite et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Strict vertical inheritance of the gut microbiota is thought not to occur in the human microbiome.
source: Indeed, strict vertical inheritance of the gut microbiota is thought not to occur in the human microbiome (Groussin et al., 2020), although recent studies using deep metagenomic microbiome sequencing have reported that in most cases the mother's dominant strains were transmitted to her child (Yassour et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In most cases the mother's dominant strains were transmitted to her child.
source: Indeed, strict vertical inheritance of the gut microbiota is thought not to occur in the human microbiome (Groussin et al., 2020), although recent studies using deep metagenomic microbiome sequencing have reported that in most cases the mother's dominant strains were transmitted to her child (Yassour et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Early gut colonizers, if retained, have the potential to exert lasting physiological effects on health and disease for most or perhaps all of adult life.
source: Therefore, early gut colonizers, if retained, do have the potential to exert lasting physiological effects on health and disease for most or perhaps all of adult life (Faith et al., 2013; Faith et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Long lasting modifications to the mature microbiota require substantial interventions, including permanent dietary changes, major changes in the health status of the host, or extensive microbial manipulations such as a long-term course of antibiotics.
source: It is also noteworthy that long lasting modifications to the mature microbiota require substantial interventions, including permanent dietary changes, major changes in the health status of the host, or extensive microbial manipulations such as a long-term course of antibiotics (Lozupone et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB) are spore-forming, Gram-positive commensal bacteria.
source: An example of a gut microbe that elicits a salient and tractable phenotype is segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB), which are spore-forming, Gram-positive commensal bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SFB.

claim: In the mouse, SFB drive the development and expansion of Th17 cells that are produced and reside in the intestinal lamina propria.
source: In the mouse, SFB drive the development and expansion of Th17 cells that are produced and reside in the intestinal lamina propria (Ivanov et al., 2009; Ivanov et al., 2008; Gaboriau-Routhiau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Th17 cells are an osteoclastogenic population of CD4+ T cells.
source: Th17 cells are an osteoclastogenic population of CD4+ T cells (Sato et al., 2006; Miossec et al., 2009) defined by their capacity to produce IL-17 (Basu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Th17 cells are defined by their capacity to produce IL-17.
source: Th17 cells are an osteoclastogenic population of CD4+ T cells (Sato et al., 2006; Miossec et al., 2009) defined by their capacity to produce IL-17 (Basu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The presence of SFB in the intestine of healthy mice leads to lower bone density.
source: The presence of SFB in the intestine of healthy mice leads to lower bone density (Hathaway-Schrader et al., 2020), which occurs via SFB-driven expansion of Th17 cells in the gut, migration of Th17 cells to the bone marrow (BM), and increased secretion of IL-17 in the BM (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SFB-induced lower bone density occurs via SFB-driven expansion of Th17 cells in the gut, migration of Th17 cells to the bone marrow (BM), and increased secretion of IL-17 in the BM.
source: The presence of SFB in the intestine of healthy mice leads to lower bone density (Hathaway-Schrader et al., 2020), which occurs via SFB-driven expansion of Th17 cells in the gut, migration of Th17 cells to the bone marrow (BM), and increased secretion of IL-17 in the BM (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In humans, about twenty non-virulent gut bacterial strains are known to induce Th17 cell differentiation.
source: Pertaining to relevance to public health, in humans, about twenty non-virulent gut bacterial strains are known to induce Th17 cell differentiation (Atarashi et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: C3H/HeN mice have higher indices of bone volume and bone structure as compared to C57BL/6 mice.
source: C3H/HeN mice have higher indices of bone volume and bone stracture as compared to C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of these mouse strains.

claim: Conventional TAC C57BL/6 mice were raised in a vivarium that contains SFB.
source: Conventional TAC C57BL/6 mice were raised in a vivarium that contains SFB, which are potent microbial inducers of Th17 cell expansion in intestinal tissue (Ivanov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: Conventional TAC C3H/HeN mice were raised in a SFB- facility.
source: Conventional TAC C3H/HeN mice were raised in a SFB- facility.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: The bacterial community structure was different in conventional C57BL/6 and C3H/HeN mice.
source: Microbiome sequencing confirmed that the bacterial community structure was different in conventional C57BL/6 and C3H/HeN mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microbiome sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SFB was absent in GF C57BL/6 mice that were colonized with C3H/HeN microbiome.
source: We also confirmed the absence of SFB in GF C57BL/6 mice that were colonized with C3H/HeN microbiome, and the presence of SFB in C3H/HeN germ-free mice that were colonized with C57BL/6 microbiome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SFB was present in C3H/HeN germ-free mice that were colonized with C57BL/6 microbiome.
source: We also confirmed the absence of SFB in GF C57BL/6 mice that were colonized with C3H/HeN microbiome, and the presence of SFB in C3H/HeN germ-free mice that were colonized with C57BL/6 microbiome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At 16 weeks of age C3H/HeN concordant mice had higher bone volume/total volume ratio (BV/TV) compared to concordant C57BL/6 mice.
source: At 16 weeks of age C3H/HeN concordant mice had higher bone volume/total volume ratio (BV/TV) compared to concordant C57BL/6 mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SFB+ mice have a lower BV/TV compared to SFB- mice.
source: SFB+ mice have a lower BV/TV compared to SFB- mice (Yu et al., 2020; Hathaway-Schrader et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Discordant C3H/HeN mice had lower femur BV/TV ratio, trabecular number (Tb.N), and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th), and higher trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) than concordant C3H/HeN mice.
source: Corroborating the relevance of SFB for skeletal maturation, we showed that the discordant C3H/HeN mice had lower femur BV/TV ratio, trabecular number (Tb.N), and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th), and higher trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) than concordant C3H/HeN mice (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 1D-G.

claim: Concordant and discordant C57BL/6 mice had similar indices of trabecular volume and structure.
source: By contrast, concordant and discordant C57BL/6 mice had similar indices of trabecular volume and structure (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 1D-G.

claim: Cortical area (Ct.Ar) and cortical thickness (Ct.Th) were higher in concordant C3H/HeN mice than in concordant C57BL/6 mice.
source: Moreover, cortical area (Ct.Ar) and cortical thickness (Ct.Th), which are indices of cortical bone structure, were higher in concordant C3H/HeN mice than in concordant C57BL/6 mice, while discordant C3H/HeN mice had lower Ct.Ar and Ct.Th than concordant C3H/HeN mice (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: Discordant C3H/HeN mice had lower Ct.Ar and Ct.Th than concordant C3H/HeN mice.
source: Moreover, cortical area (Ct.Ar) and cortical thickness (Ct.Th), which are indices of cortical bone structure, were higher in concordant C3H/HeN mice than in concordant C57BL/6 mice, while discordant C3H/HeN mice had lower Ct.Ar and Ct.Th than concordant C3H/HeN mice (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: Ct.Ar and Ct.Th were higher in discordant C57BL/6 mice than in concordant C57BL/6 mice.
source: Analysis of C57BL/6 mice cortical structure revealed that Ct.Ar and Ct.Th were higher in discordant than in concordant mice (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: TAC C57BL/6 microbiome worsens trabecular and cortical bone maturation.
source: Together, these findings indicate that TAC C57BL/6 microbiome worsen trabecular and cortical bone maturation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on bone structure.

claim: Serum CTX was higher in concordant C57BL/6 mice than in concordant C3H/HeN mice.
source: Mechanistic studies revealed that serum CTX, a marker of bone resorption, was higher in concordant C57BL/6 mice than in concordant C3H/HeN mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data measuring serum CTX levels.

claim: C3H/HeN microbiome lowered CTX levels in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Moreover, C3H/HeN microbiome lowered CTX levels in C57BL/6 mice, while C57BL/6 microbiome increased bone resorption in C3H/HeN mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: C57BL/6 microbiome increased bone resorption in C3H/HeN mice.
source: Moreover, C3H/HeN microbiome lowered CTX levels in C57BL/6 mice, while C57BL/6 microbiome increased bone resorption in C3H/HeN mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: All groups of mice had similar serum levels of osteocalcin.
source: By contrast, all groups of mice had similar serum levels of osteocalcin, a marker of bone formation (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The number of PP Th17 cells and the levels of small intestine (SI) tissue Il17a transcripts were higher in all groups of mice with SFB+ microbiome than in those with SFB- microbiome.
source: We confirmed that the number of PP Th17 cells and the levels of small intestine (SI) tissue Il17a transcripts were higher in all groups of mice with SFB+ microbiome than in those with SFB- microbiome (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The number of Th17 cells and the levels of Il17a mRNA in the BM were higher in all mice with an SFB+ microbiome, as compared to those with SFB– microbiome.
source: In addition, the number of Th17 cells and the levels of Il17a mRNA in the BM were also higher in all mice with an SFB+ microbiome, as compared to those with SFB– microbiome (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: The levels of Tnfa mRNA were higher in the BM and SI of mice with SFB+ microbiome.
source: Accordingly, we found the levels of Tnfa mRNA were higher in the BM and SI and of mice with SFB+ microbiome (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: BM Rankl (Tnfsf11) was higher in mice with SFB+ microbiome.
source: BM Receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand (Rankl), also known as tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11 (Tnfsf11) was higher in mice with SFB+ microbiome (Figure 2I), although SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups.
source: BM Receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand (Rankl), also known as tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11 (Tnfsf11) was higher in mice with SFB+ microbiome (Figure 2I), although SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The signal to expand BM Th17 cells originates in the intestine, and requires Th17 cell-inducing bacteria, such as SFB to be a component of the microbiome.
source: These data suggest that the signal to expand BM Th17 cells originates in the intestine, and requires Th17 cell-inducing bacteria, such as SFB to be a component of the microbiome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on Th17 cells.

claim: Acquisition of maternal microbiome at birth affects the postnatal skeletal development of the offspring regardless of its genetic strain.
source: Critically, these data show proof of principle that acquisition of maternal microbiome at birth affects the postnatal skeletal development of the offspring regardless of its genetic strain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on maternal microbiome transfer.

claim: Cohabitation is a key non-genomic factor that influences the development over time of species structure in the microbiota of humans and mice.
source: Cohabitation is a key non-genomic factor that influences the development over time of species structure in the microbiota of humans (Faith et al., 2013) and mice (Robertson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: JAX and TAC mice have distinct microbiome composition and diversity.
source: Confirming earlier reports (Ivanov et al., 2009), we found JAX and TAC mice to have distinct microbiome composition and diversity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microbiome sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TAC mice were SFB+ while JAX mice were SFB-.
source: Importantly, while TAC mice were SFB+, JAX mice were SFB- (Figure 3C), a finding concordant with previous reports (Farkas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C and citations to previous research.

claim: Co-housing of JAX and TAC mice equalized the composition of the microbiome, and lead to SFB colonization within the JAX mice.
source: As expected, co-housing of JAX and TAC mice equalized the composition of the microbiome, and lead to SFB colonization within the JAX mice (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microbiome sequencing and qPCR data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: JAX C57BL/6 mice that were housed alone had a higher femoral BV/TV, Tb.N and Tb.Th and lower Tb.Sp than TAC mice housed alone.
source: JAX C57BL/6 mice that were housed alone had a higher femoral BV/TV, Tb.N and Tb.Th and lower Tb.Sp than TAC mice housed alone (Figure 3D–G), although they did have similar cortical structure (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 3D-G.

claim: JAX and TAC mice housed alone had similar cortical structure.
source: JAX C57BL/6 mice that were housed alone had a higher femoral BV/TV, Tb.N and Tb.Th and lower Tb.Sp than TAC mice housed alone (Figure 3D–G), although they did have similar cortical structure (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: Co-housing of JAX mice with TAC mice resulted in the equalization of all indices of trabecular volume and structure.
source: Co-housing of JAX mice with TAC mice resulted in the equalization of all indices of trabecular volume and structure, although it did not affect cortical bone indices (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 3D-I.

claim: Co-housing did not affect cortical bone indices.
source: Co-housing of JAX mice with TAC mice resulted in the equalization of all indices of trabecular volume and structure, although it did not affect cortical bone indices (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 3D-I.

claim: TAC mice housed alone had higher levels of serum CTX than JAX mice housed alone.
source: TAC mice housed alone had higher levels of serum CTX than JAX mice housed alone (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Co-housing of JAX and TAC mice increased the serum levels of CTX in JAX mice, leading to the equalization of CTX levels.
source: Co-housing of JAX and TAC mice increased the serum levels of CTX in JAX mice, leading to the equalization of CTX levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data on serum CTX levels.

claim: All groups of mice in the cohabitation experiment had similar levels of serum osteocalcin.
source: By contrast, all groups of mice had similar levels of serum osteocalcin (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Post-natal skeletal development is influenced by cohabitation via a microbiome dependent mechanism that affects bone resorption.
source: These findings indicate that post-natal skeletal development is infleunced by cohabitation via a microbiome dependent mechanism that affects bone resorption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cohabitation experimental data.

claim: TAC mice had a higher number of PP and BM Th17 cells and higher expressions of SI and BM Il17a transcripts compared to JAX mice.
source: We found that TAC mice had a higher number of PP and BM Th17 cells and higher expressions of SI and BM Il17a transcripts compared to JAX mice (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figures 4A-E.

claim: Co-housing resulted in an increase in Th17 cells and Il17a mRNA in JAX mice.
source: Co-housing resulted in an increase in Th17 cells and Il17a mRNA in JAX mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data.

claim: At the end of the cohabitation period, Th17 cells and Il17a transcript were similar in gut tissues and BM of TAC mice and cohoused JAX mice compared to JAX mice housed alone.
source: As a result, at the end of the cohabitation period, Th17 cells and Il17a transcript were similar in gut tissues and BM of TAC mice and cohoused JAX mice compared to JAX mice housed alone (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figures 4A-E.

claim: TAC mice housed alone had higher expression of SI and BM Tnfa than JAX mice housed alone.
source: In addition, TAC mice housed alone had higher expression of SI and BM Tnfa than JAX mice housed alone, while co-housing of the two groups increased the levels of Tnfa transcripts in JAX mice, up to levels of TAC mice (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Co-housing of the two groups increased the levels of Tnfa transcripts in JAX mice, up to levels of TAC mice.
source: In addition, TAC mice housed alone had higher expression of SI and BM Tnfa than JAX mice housed alone, while co-housing of the two groups increased the levels of Tnfa transcripts in JAX mice, up to levels of TAC mice (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups in the cohabitation experiment.
source: Finally, while SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups (Figure 4H), expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM was higher in TAC mice than in JAX mice housed alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM was higher in TAC mice than in JAX mice housed alone.
source: Finally, while SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups (Figure 4H), expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM was higher in TAC mice than in JAX mice housed alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data.

claim: BM Tnfsf11 mRNA levels increased in JAX mice as a result of co-housing with TAC mice.
source: However, BM Tnfsf11 mRNA levels increased in JAX mice as a result of co-housing with TAC mice (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Co-housing of JAX mice with TAC mice induced bone loss in JAX mice by expanding BM Th17 cells and increasing osteoclastogenic cytokine levels.
source: These data suggest that co-housing of JAX mice with TAC mice induced bone loss in JAX mice by expanding BM Th17 cells and increasing osteoclastogenic cytokine levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on cohabitation effects.

claim: The gut microbiota in mature animals and humans is resistant to colonization by new organisms.
source: Although the gut microbiota in mature animals and humans is resistant to colonization by new organisms, extensive and prolonged microbicidal interventions such as a long-term course of antibiotics may elicit enduring changes (Yatsunenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Extensive and prolonged microbicidal interventions such as a long-term course of antibiotics may elicit enduring changes to the gut microbiota.
source: Although the gut microbiota in mature animals and humans is resistant to colonization by new organisms, extensive and prolonged microbicidal interventions such as a long-term course of antibiotics may elicit enduring changes (Yatsunenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Donor C57BL/6 and C3H/HeN mice had distinct microbiome composition and diversity.
source: Analysis showed that donor C57BL/6 and C3H/HeN mice had distinct microbiome composition and diversity, and that FMT led to the establishment of the donor microbiome in the host mouse (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microbiome sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FMT led to the establishment of the donor microbiome in the host mouse.
source: Analysis showed that donor C57BL/6 and C3H/HeN mice had distinct microbiome composition and diversity, and that FMT led to the establishment of the donor microbiome in the host mouse (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microbiome sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SFB was present in donor C57BL/6 mice.
source: We confirmed that SFB was present in donor C57BL/6 mice, and that antibiotic treated mice subjected to FMT with fecal material from these mice were also SFB+(Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Antibiotic treated mice subjected to FMT with fecal material from C57BL/6 mice were also SFB+.
source: We confirmed that SFB was present in donor C57BL/6 mice, and that antibiotic treated mice subjected to FMT with fecal material from these mice were also SFB+(Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Donor C3H/HeN mice had higher femoral BV/TV, Tb.N, Tb.Th and lower Tb.Sp compared to C57BL/6 mice.
source: In-vitro µCT analysis showed that donor C3H/HeN mice had higher femoral BV/TV, Tb.N, Tb.Th and lower Tb.Sp compared to C57BL/6 mice (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 5D-G.

claim: C3H/HeN mice had higher indices of cortical structure compared to C57BL/6 mice.
source: C3H/HeN mice also had higher indices of cortical structure compared to C57BL/6 mice (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 5H and 5I.

claim: FMT from donor C57BL/6 mice to antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice altered all indices of trabecular volume and structure in the recipient C3H/HeN mice.
source: FMT from donor C57BL/6 mice to antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice altered all indices of trabecular volume and structure in the recipient C3H/HeN mice (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 5D-G.

claim: FMT from C57BL/6 mice to antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice induced cortical bone loss in the recipient C3H/HeN mice.
source: In addition, FMT from C57BL/6 mice to antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice induced cortical bone loss in the recipient C3H/HeN mice (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 5H and 5I.

claim: FMT from donor C3H/HeN mice did not affect indices of trabecular and cortical bone in recipient C57BL/6 mice.
source: Conversely, FMT from donor C3H/HeN mice did not affect indices of trabecular and cortical bone in recipient C57BL/6 mice (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by µCT data shown in Figures 5D-I.

claim: Gut microbiota of C57BL/6 mice has modulatory influences on both trabecular and cortical bone structure.
source: These data suggested that gut microbiota of C57BL/6 mice has modulatory influences on both trabecular and cortical bone structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FMT experimental data.

claim: Serum levels of CTX were significantly higher in antibiotic treated C57BL/6 mice and C3H/HeN mice colonized with C57BL/6 microbiome.
source: Analysis showed that serum levels of CTX were significantly higher in antibiotic treated C57BL/6 mice and C3H/HeN mice colonized with C57BL/6 microbiome (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: FMT had no effect on the levels of osteocalcin in all experimental groups.
source: However, FMT had no effect on the levels of osteocalcin in all experimental groups (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The bone loss that occurred following the transfer of a C57BL/6 microbiome to recipient mice was due to increasing bone resorption.
source: These data indicate that the bone loss that occurred following the transfer of a C57BL/6 microbiome to recipient mice was due to increasing bone resorption.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FMT experimental data on bone turnover markers.

claim: C57BL/6 donor mice had higher numbers of PP and BM Th17 cells, and higher expression of Il17a transcripts compared to C3H/HeN donor mice.
source: Additional studies revealed that C57BL/6 donor mice had higher numbers of PP and BM Th17 cells, and higher expression of Il17a transcripts compared to C3H/HeN donor mice (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figures 6A-E.

claim: FMT of fecal material from C57BL/6 donor mice to antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice resulted in increased Th17 cell numbers and Il17a transcript in recipient mice.
source: FMT of fecal material from C57BL/6 donor mice to antibiotic treated to C3H/HeN mice resulted in increased Th17 cell numbers and Il17a transcript in recipient mice (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figures 6A-E.

claim: Antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice colonized with fecal material from C57BL/6 donor had higher levels of Tnfa mRNA in the SI and BM compared to donor C3H/HeN mice.
source: In addition, antibiotic treated C3H/HeN mice colonized with fecal material from C57BL/6 donor had higher levels of Tnfa mRNA in the SI and BM compared to donor C3H/HeN mice (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups in the FMT experiment.
source: While SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups (Figure 6H), expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM was higher in donor C57BL/6 TAC than in C3H/HeN mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM was higher in donor C57BL/6 TAC than in C3H/HeN mice.
source: While SI Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were similar in all groups (Figure 6H), expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM was higher in donor C57BL/6 TAC than in C3H/HeN mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data.

claim: BM Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were increased in antibiotic treated mice colonized with C57BL/6.
source: Moreover, BM Tnfsf11 mRNA levels were increased in antibiotic treated mice colonized with C57BL/6 (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The transfer of the C57BL/6 TAC microbiome to an antibiotic treated mouse of a different strain resulted in the induction of an inflammatory environment that led to increased bone resorption and net bone loss.
source: These data indicate that the transfer of the C57BL/6 TAC microbiome to an antibiotic treated mouse of a different strain resulted in the induction of an inflammatory environment that led to increased bone resorption and net bone loss.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FMT experimental data.

claim: Colonization following a major disruption to the microbiome can change the microbiome composition and induce skeletal phenotypic alterations.
source: The data also suggest that colonization following a major disruption to the microbiome can change the microbiome composition and induce skeletal phenotypic alterations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FMT experimental data.

claim: The gut microbiome shapes the acquisition of bone volume, structure and turnover when acquired by newborn mice via vertical transfer from the mother or by young mice via co-housing with other mice.
source: We showed that the gut microbiome shapes the acquisition of bone volume, structure and turnover when acquired by newborn mice via vertical transfer from the mother or by young mice via co-housing with other mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Replacement of the original established microbiome with a new microbiome via treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics followed by FMT also conditioned skeletal maturation.
source: Replacement of the original established microbiome with a new microbiome via treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics followed by FMT, also conditioned skeletal maturation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Transmission of gut microbes, and in particular of SFB, lead to the stimulation of bone resorption in recipient mice of the same, or different genetic strain.
source: Transmission of gut microbes, and in particular of SFB, lead to the stimulation of bone resorption in recipient mice of the same, or different genetic strain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The gut microbiome acts as a major non-genomic heritable factor in the transmission of bone phenotypes, including from mother to offspring.
source: Moreover, the gut microbiome was found to act as a major non-genomic heritable factor in the transmission of bone phenotypes, including from mother to offspring.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The microbiome is a communicable regulator of bone development.
source: Together, these data showed that the microbiome is a communicable regulator of bone development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: IL-17 stimulates the release of further inflammatory cytokines.
source: IL-17 stimulates the release of further inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about IL-17.

claim: IL-17 is known to induce TNFSF11 production by osteoblasts and osteocytes.
source: IL-17 is known to induce TNFSF11 production by osteoblasts and osteocytes (Lee, 2013; Li, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Osteoblasts and osteocytes might be the source of TNFSF11 in the BM of mice in response to elevated levels of BM IL-17.
source: Therefore, it is likely that osteoblasts and osteocytes might be the source of TNFSF11 in the BM of mice in response to elevated levels of BM IL-17, and that the absence of these lineages and other TNFSF11 producing cells sensitive to IL-17 in the intestine may explain the inability of IL-17 to stimulate TNFSF11 production in the gut.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: The absence of osteoblasts, osteocytes and other TNFSF11 producing cells sensitive to IL-17 in the intestine may explain the inability of IL-17 to stimulate TNFSF11 production in the gut.
source: Therefore, it is likely that osteoblasts and osteocytes might be the source of TNFSF11 in the BM of mice in response to elevated levels of BM IL-17, and that the absence of these lineages and other TNFSF11 producing cells sensitive to IL-17 in the intestine may explain the inability of IL-17 to stimulate TNFSF11 production in the gut.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: The effects of the microbiome on skeletal development were more potent in trabecular bone than in cortical bone.
source: It should also be noted that the effects of the microbiome on skeletal development were more potent in trabecular bone than in cortical bone.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The microbiome does not regulate cortical bone.
source: This is consistent with previous reports where we found the microbiome not to regulate cortical bone (Li et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Tyagi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: The microbiome regulates bone acquisition mostly via T cells.
source: This is likely to reflect the fact that the microbiome regulates bone acquisition mostly via T cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data and previous knowledge.

claim: T cells reside in the BM, where they have physical access to trabecular bone cells.
source: These cells reside in the BM, where they have physical access to trabecular bone cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T cell localization.

claim: Cytokines secreted by T cells are present in relative high concentration in the BM, where they can affect bone cells and their precursors.
source: In addition, cytokines secreted by T cells are present in relative high concentration in the BM, where they can affect bone cells and their precursors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cytokine distribution.

claim: T cells have minimal physical access to cortical bone.
source: By contrast, T cells have minimal physical access to cortical bone.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T cell localization.

claim: In each of the three experimental models utilized in the current study, the microbiome regulated skeletal development by modulating bone resorption without affecting bone formation.
source: In each of the three experimental models utilized in the current study, the microbiome regulated skeletal development by modulating bone resorption without affecting bone formation.
evidence: This is a summary observation from the experimental data.

claim: The capacity of IL-17 to blunt bone formation might have been offset by gut microbes that stimulate bone formation such as bacteria that generate short chain fatty acids.
source: The reason for this phenomenon remains unknown, although it is tempting to speculate that the capacity of IL-17 to blunt bone formation (Kim et al., 2014) might have been offset by gut microbes that stimulate bone formation such as bacteria that generate short chain fatty acids (Zaiss et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on citations to previous research.

claim: The gut microbiome is a non-genomic heritable factor that contributes to the variance of bone volume, structure and turnover within populations.
source: In summary, our data showed that the gut microbiome is a non-genomic heritable factor that contributes to the variance of bone volume, structure and turnover within populations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The specific effects of the microbiome on bone depend on its diversity and composition.
source: The specific effects of the microbiome on bone depend on its diversity and composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The presence in the gut microbiome of saprophytic strains capable of expanding intestinal Th17 cell in healthy individuals is likely to be a predictor of suboptimal skeletal development and low peak bone mass.
source: The presence in the gut microbiome of saprophytic strains capable of expanding intestinal Th17 cell in healthy individuals it is likely to a predictor of suboptimal skeletal development and low peak bone mass.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The transfer of microbes that trigger the expansion of gut Th17 cells during FMT from healthy donors to recipients could lead to lower bone density in recipients.
source: Furthermore, the findings of this study have significant implications to the practice of FMT from healthy donors to recipients, where the transfer of microbes that trigger the expansion of gut Th17 cells could lead to lower bone density in recipients.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: The method or timing of microbiome transfer is a window of opportunity to apply bacteriotherapeutic interventions to overcome suboptimal skeletal maturation.
source: On the other hand, we also identified the method or timing of microbiome transfer as a window of opportunity to apply bacteriotherapeutic interventions to overcome suboptimal skeletal maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential therapeutic applications based on the experimental findings.

claim: The most potent human Th17 cell-inducing bacteria are Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus faecalis and Acinetobacter baumanii.
source: Among them the most are Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus faecalis and Acinetobacter baumanii (Atarashi et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The gut microbiota of healthy people shows resilience and a capacity for recovery following antibiotic treatment.
source: Despite reports that the gut microbiota of healthy people shows resilience and a capacity for recovery following antibiotic treatment (Palleja et al., 2018), we showed that FMT immediately after antibiotic treatment potently modified post-natal bone development phenotype in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: FMT immediately after antibiotic treatment potently modified post-natal bone development phenotype in mice.
source: Despite reports that the gut microbiota of healthy people shows resilience and a capacity for recovery following antibiotic treatment (Palleja et al., 2018), we showed that FMT immediately after antibiotic treatment potently modified post-natal bone development phenotype in mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the FMT experimental data.

claim: Following a course of broad-spectrum of antibiotics, the microbiome may be modified by FMT to introduce bacterial strains that may elicit modulatory effects on bone health and disease.
source: Our observations are evidence that following a course of broad-spectrum of antibiotics, the microbiome may indeed be modified by FMT to introduce bacterial strains that may elicit modulatory effects on bone health and disease.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FMT experimental data.

claim: In the experimental approach using mice, 4 weeks colonization of microbiome materials introduced by FMT was sufficient to elicit a phenotype.
source: However, in our approach using mice, we show that 4 weeks colonization of microbiome materials introduced by FMT was sufficient to elicit a phenotype.
evidence: This is an observation from the FMT experimental data.

claim: The acquisition and establishment of a Th17 cell expanding microbe early in life may have pernicious effects on post-natal bone metabolism over an entire lifetime.
source: Nevertheless, since the lifespans of humans are considerably longer than experimental science timeframes, which was up to 8 weeks in the models outlined in this manuscript, the acquisition and establishment of a Th17 cell expanding microbe early in life may have pernicious effects on post-natal bone metabolism over an entire lifetime.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the experimental findings to human health.

claim: Increased expression of Il17a in the gut and the BM was associated with increased expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM but not in the gut.
source: An interesting finding of our studies was that increased expression of Il17a in the gut and the BM was associated with increased expression of Tnfsf11 in the BM but not in the gut.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.
